fetched_contents.text: Flock size during rearing affects pullet behavioural synchrony and spatial clustering Animals are often synchronised in their behaviour, with costs and benefits varying according to group size and the behaviour being performed. Making decisions about optimal allocation and distribution of resources to animals in our care therefore poses theoretical and practical challenges. We investigated group size effects on behavioural synchrony and spatial clustering during daytime in pullets of a commercial laying hen strain reared until 18 weeks of age in groups of 15, 30, 60 and 120 (four replicates of each group size). Feeder, drinker, perch and litter space (i.e. floor space allowance) per bird, were constant across group sizes and all resources were continuously available. Even though the absolute numbers of birds performing the same behaviour at the same time or being located together at the same resource patch increased with increasing group size, the relative degree of synchrony of feeding, drinking, perching and preening across the whole flock decreased exponentially with increasing group size (P < 0.001 for all behaviours) as did the relative degree of clustering at the same resource patch (P < 0.001 for the same four behaviours). Preening was the most synchronous behaviour (more than twice that of the least synchronised behaviour, perching), and feeding the most clustered in space (three times more clustered than the other behaviours). These results imply that it is more important to provide sufficient resource space for all birds to perform daytime activities simultaneously when kept in the smaller group sizes typical of cages, than in the larger flocks typical of birds kept in floor pens and aviaries. fetched_contents.text: Do Laying Hens Form Stable Social Networks?—A Case Study Article Menu Font Type: Arial Georgia Verdana Line Spacing:    Column Width:    Open AccessCase Report by Louise Hedlund , Dominic Wright and Per Jensen IFM Biology, AVIAN Behavioural Physiology and Genomics Group, Linköping University, 581 83 Linköping, Sweden Author to whom correspondence should be addressed. Submission received: 22 November 2024 / Revised: 20 December 2024 / Accepted: 9 January 2025 / Published: 30 January 2025 Abstract A social network is a group of individuals forming a non-random social structure where the number of interactions systematically vary among individuals. The Red Junglefowl, the ancestor of all domesticated chickens, has been shown to form social structures within a larger group; however, how poultry in egg production are socially organised is poorly understood. Egg layers in groups of thousands of individuals are suggested to either, just as Red Junglefowl, form subgroups or to lose social affiliations and replace these with a system of social tolerance. In this case study, a stable group of 20 laying hens with known genetic relationships housed in an outdoor aviary were observed for 3 h per day, during 20 days, in order to determine the social structure in the group. Social affiliations and centralisation measurements were assessed by proximity. The results show that some individuals were consistently more centralised compared to others, which indicates a stable individual variation in sociality. Furthermore, no individual spent more than 10% of her total number of interactions with a particular individual, i.e., little consistency in social affiliations could be found. The results of this case study support the theory of a higher social tolerance rather than a consistent social organisation in domesticated egg layers. 1. Introduction A social network is a group of individuals forming a non-random social structure where the number of interactions systematically vary among individuals [1,2]. Close associations between animals are beneficial from an evolutionary standpoint. For example, it could minimise intra-group aggression [3] and may allow animals to reach goals that would not be otherwise attainable [2]. Affiliations also relate to mating success [4,5,6,7] and are suggested to increase the motivation for reciprocal altruism in several species [2]. In chickens, social affiliations have been shown to be an effective strategy to avoid harassment from males [7] and reduce aggression within a group [8]. The ancestor of the domesticated laying hen, the Red Junglefowl, lives in smaller groups of about 10 animals [9,10,11]. In larger groups, they form subgroups within the flock, in particular, female–female pairs [12], that are associated with age and rank [7]. However, the every-day life of a domesticated layer in the egg industry differs vastly from that of their ancestor. The layers used in egg production are kept in large industrial production environments, where one flock normally consists of thousands of individuals [13]. In Sweden, where this study was performed, there are flocks with up to at least 69,700 individuals [14], and the largest farm in Sweden has permission to hold 2.9 million fowl [15]. Although the bird density is regulated by Swedish animal legislation, flock size is not [16]. Some evidence indicates that layers in large flocks, just as the Junglefowl, form subgroups and restrict their movements to certain smaller areas [17,18], and that they maintain somewhat stable relationships in terms of proximity [19,20]. However, they seem to have a poorer social learning capacity than their ancestors [21], and one suggestion is that they have, rather than a systematic social structure, an overall high social tolerance without the necessity to recognise each other individually [8,22,23,24]. # How flock size affects behavioral synchronization

The evidence points to behavioral synchronization as a phenomenon shaped by group size, with synchronization measured through repeated timing or spatial overlap across flocks or individuals. In the direct experimental evidence, Keeling et al. studied pullets reared in groups of 15, 30, 60, and 120 birds, and they quantified synchronization as the relative degree of synchrony of feeding, drinking, perching, and preening across the whole flock [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. The study also measured spatial clustering at the same resource patch, using the same four behaviors as a measure of spatial concentration [N3-F1]. This is important because it means the synchronization indicators are not abstract; they are tied to real-time, observable actions that can be compared across flocks [N3-F1].

## Which behavioral indicators are used to measure synchronization?

The direct experimental evidence uses feeding, drinking, perching, and preening as the main behavioral indicators for synchronization [N3-F1]. In addition, the review context notes that behavioral synchronization can be assessed by qualitative behavioral assessment (QBA) in poultry, though it is difficult to apply because of flock homogeneity [N5-F2]. The review also mentions that preening is the most synchronized behavior in laying hens and daytime perching the least [N5-F2]. This implies that synchronization is not measured as a single binary trait but as a relative ranking across behaviors, with some behaviors being more synchronized than others.

## How flock size changes the speed or strength of synchronization

The key result from the experimental study is that synchronization decreased exponentially with increasing group size [N3-F1]. The abstract says, “the relative degree of synchrony [...] decreased exponentially with increasing group size” for all four behaviors, and the same was true for spatial clustering [N3-F1]. This means that as flocks grow, the speed or strength of synchronization does not simply diminish slightly; it declines sharply. The study also notes that although absolute numbers of birds performing the same behavior at the same time or being together at the same resource patch increased with group size, the relative synchrony still fell [N3-F1]. In other words, more birds doing the same thing together does not necessarily mean stronger synchronization; the proportion of the flock engaged in synchronized behavior becomes less concentrated as group size increases.

## Whether synchronization is stronger in smaller or larger flocks

Based on the direct evidence, synchronization is stronger in smaller flocks. The exponential decrease in relative synchrony with increasing group size means that smaller groups have higher synchrony than larger groups [N3-F1]. The same study also says that the results imply that sufficient resource space is more important in smaller group sizes typical of cages than in larger flocks typical of floor pens and aviaries [N3-F1]. This further supports the idea that smaller flocks naturally support stronger synchronization because the same resources are not crowded out by too many individuals.

## Whether synchronization mechanisms depend on social hierarchy

The evidence is suggestive but not definitive. The social-networks review notes that chickens form a social hierarchy, often referred to as the “pecking order,” and that the hierarchical matrix can be used to determine dominance hierarchy based on the proportion of instances when each hen was the dominant or subordinate bird [N1-R2]. It also states that aggressive dominance can decrease behavioral complexity on subordinates through synchronization of locomotor activities [N1-R3]. The direct experimental study does not explicitly test social hierarchy as a variable, but the social-networks context indicates that synchronization may be linked to social structure and that dominance relationships can influence how individuals behave together [N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-F2]. Therefore, the evidence supports the idea that synchronization mechanisms can depend on social hierarchy, but the direct experimental evidence provided here does not itself establish hierarchy as the causal mechanism.

## Overall conclusion

The strongest-supported conclusion from the provided evidence is that flock size reduces the relative strength and speed of synchronization, especially in the behaviors studied by Keeling et al. The study is experimental, and it measures synchronization through repeated behavioral timing and resource-use patterns rather than only social interactions [N3-R1][N3-F1]. The broader context adds that social hierarchy and network structure are relevant to synchronization, but the direct evidence here does not prove hierarchy as the mechanism [N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-F2]. For the current question, the evidence supports stronger synchronization in smaller flocks and weaker synchronization in larger flocks [N3-F1].

# How flock size affects behavioral synchronization

The evidence points to behavioral synchronization as a phenomenon shaped by group size, with synchronization measured through repeated timing or spatial overlap across flocks or individuals. In the direct experimental evidence, Keeling et al. studied pullets reared in groups of 15, 30, 60, and 120 birds, and they quantified synchronization as the relative degree of synchrony of feeding, drinking, perching, and preening across the whole flock [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F1]. The study also measured spatial clustering at the same resource patch, using the same four behaviors as a measure of spatial concentration [N3-F1]. This is important because it means the synchronization indicators are not abstract; they are tied to real-time, observable actions that can be compared across flocks [N3-F1].

## Which behavioral indicators are used to measure synchronization?

The direct experimental evidence uses feeding, drinking, perching, and preening as the main behavioral indicators for synchronization [N3-F1]. In addition, the review context notes that behavioral synchronization can be assessed by qualitative behavioral assessment (QBA) in poultry, though it is difficult to apply because of flock homogeneity [N5-F2]. The review also mentions that preening is the most synchronized behavior in laying hens and daytime perching the least [N5-F2]. This implies that synchronization is not measured as a single binary trait but as a relative ranking across behaviors, with some behaviors being more synchronized than others.

## How flock size changes the speed or strength of synchronization

The key result from the experimental study is that synchronization decreased exponentially with increasing group size [N3-F1]. The abstract says, “the relative degree of synchrony [...] decreased exponentially with increasing group size” for all four behaviors, and the same was true for spatial clustering [N3-F1]. This means that as flocks grow, the speed or strength of synchronization does not simply diminish slightly; it declines sharply. The study also notes that although absolute numbers of birds performing the same behavior at the same time or being together at the same resource patch increased with group size, the relative synchrony still fell [N3-F1]. In other words, more birds doing the same thing together does not necessarily mean stronger synchronization; the proportion of the flock engaged in synchronized behavior becomes less concentrated as group size increases.

## Whether synchronization is stronger in smaller or larger flocks

Based on the direct evidence, synchronization is stronger in smaller flocks. The exponential decrease in relative synchrony with increasing group size means that smaller groups have higher synchrony than larger groups [N3-F1]. The same study also says that the results imply that sufficient resource space is more important in smaller group sizes typical of cages than in larger flocks typical of floor pens and aviaries [N3-F1]. This further supports the idea that smaller flocks naturally support stronger synchronization because the same resources are not crowded out by too many individuals.

## Whether synchronization mechanisms depend on social hierarchy

The evidence is suggestive but not definitive. The social-networks review notes that chickens form a social hierarchy, often referred to as the “pecking order,” and that the hierarchical matrix can be used to determine dominance hierarchy based on the proportion of instances when each hen was the dominant or subordinate bird [N1-R2]. It also states that aggressive dominance can decrease behavioral complexity on subordinates through synchronization of locomotor activities [N1-R3]. The direct experimental study does not explicitly test social hierarchy as a variable, but the social-networks context indicates that synchronization may be linked to social structure and that dominance relationships can influence how individuals behave together [N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-F2]. Therefore, the evidence supports the idea that synchronization mechanisms can depend on social hierarchy, but the direct experimental evidence provided here does not itself establish hierarchy as the causal mechanism.

## Overall conclusion

The strongest-supported conclusion from the provided evidence is that flock size reduces the relative strength and speed of synchronization, especially in the behaviors studied by Keeling et al. The study is experimental, and it measures synchronization through repeated behavioral timing and resource-use patterns rather than only social interactions [N3-R1][N3-F1]. The broader context adds that social hierarchy and network structure are relevant to synchronization, but the direct evidence here does not prove hierarchy as the mechanism [N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-F2]. For the current question, the evidence supports stronger synchronization in smaller flocks and weaker synchronization in larger flocks [N3-F1].
